subtype: Approach: win the argument with facts and links [Pitfall]
passage:
Dear Deepak Mama,

I want to tell you what I did, because I keep going over it. For a week after the dinner I sent you articles: eleven links, three charts, and one table I made myself. I wrote 'see, here are the figures' under each one. I honestly thought that once you saw the evidence, you would have to agree.

Every link came back with a longer message from you, and a sharper one. On Sunday you left the table before the sweets were served. Mummy told me she felt caught between us.

I wanted to be right more than I wanted to hear you. I'm sorry it turned into a contest. I would like to start again with a cup of tea.

Parul

qa.q: How many links did Parul send Deepak Mama?
qa.a: Eleven links, plus three charts and one table.

qa.q: Why did Parul send so many articles?
qa.a: Parul wanted to win, believing that evidence alone would force agreement, so the sending grew out of a wish to be right.

qa.q: What could Parul do instead of forwarding more evidence, and why?
qa.a: Parul could ask Deepak Mama about his worries and listen before offering any facts, because facts are heard better once a person feels understood.

qa.q: How does Deepak Mama's Sunday exit show what the articles did to him?
qa.a: Leaving before the sweets suggests he felt attacked and defensive rather than persuaded, so each fact made the debate a contest of who was right.

grounding: The student forwards statistics and articles to prove the uncle wrong, and each fact hardens resistance.

subtype: Approach: win the argument with facts and links [Pitfall]
passage:
Nilesh, you asked why I'm not in the family group any more. I'm Reena. I left. Here's the silly story.
Chacha posted something about the new farm policy that I knew was wrong. So I replied with a chart. He replied with a video. I sent three articles and a government report with the exact page highlighted. He sent a forward from 'a retired officer'. By midnight I'd sent eleven links. I was so sure one of them would make him say, 'Okay, beta, you're right.'
He never did. Each link made him dig in harder. By the end he wasn't even talking about the policy. He was saying, 'You think you're smarter than all of us because you go to a big college.' And honestly? That's what it had become. A fight about who was smarter.
Mummy called the next morning and said Chacha was hurt. I left the group that afternoon.
The facts were right, Nilesh. That's the annoying part. They just didn't matter the way I thought.

qa.q: How many links had Reena sent by midnight?
What did Reena hope for with each link sent?
qa.a: Reena was sure and eager, expecting one of them to make Chacha admit defeat.

qa.q: What could Reena try instead next time?
qa.a: Ask Chacha what worries him about the policy and listen, rather than trying to win with links.

qa.q: How might Chacha have felt as the links kept coming?
qa.a: Belittled and hurt, feeling talked down to by a younger relative, which made him dig in harder.

grounding: Shows a student trying to prove an uncle wrong with statistics and links, which hardens his resistance as it becomes a contest.

subtype: Approach: win the argument with facts and links [Pitfall]

I'm Thomas, Chandrika's cousin, and I was sitting across the table at our grandfather's birthday lunch when it started.
Uncle Mathew said something about fuel prices and the government, and Chandrika put down her fork. 'That's not true, uncle. Let me show you.' She pulled up a chart on her phone. He waved it away. She found a news report. He said the news lies. She read out numbers from a ministry website, faster and louder.
I watched his face. It wasn't changing his mind. It was hardening. By the third website he had stopped arguing about fuel at all. 'You young people think a phone makes you wise,' he said, and the whole table went silent.
Chandrika said, 'I'm just giving you facts,' and I believe she meant it. But the more right she was, the more he dug in.
Grandfather cut the cake early. Uncle Mathew left before tea. Chandrika sat on the steps afterwards, scrolling through her charts, as if still trying to win.

qa.q: What did Uncle Mathew say about the news report?
What does Chandrika scrolling through her charts afterwards suggest?
qa.a: She still feels frustrated and wants to be proven right, not yet seeing why the facts failed.

qa.q: What could Chandrika try differently with Uncle Mathew?
qa.a: Ask what worries him about fuel prices and listen first, instead of turning lunch into a contest of charts.

qa.q: How does the lunch look to Thomas?
qa.a: Thomas watches the uncle's face harden with each fact and sees the argument turn into a matter of pride, not fuel prices.

grounding: Shows a student using charts and statistics to prove an uncle wrong at a family lunch, which only hardens his resistance.
